prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Genial poets, pink-faced earnest wits— you have given the world some choice morsels, gobbets of language presented as one presents T-bone steak and Cherries Jubilee. Goodbye, goodbye, I don’t care if I never taste your fine food again, neutral fellows, seers of every side. Tolerance, what crimes are committed in your name. And you, good women, bakers of nicest bread, blood donors. Your crumbs choke me, I would not want a drop of your blood in me, it is pumped by weak hearts, perfect pulses that never falter: irresponsive to nightmare reality. It is my brothers, my sisters, whose blood spurts out and stops forever because you choose to believe it is not your business. Goodbye, goodbye, your poems shut their little mouths, your loaves grow moldy, a gulf has split the ground between us, and you won’t wave, you’re looking another way. We shan’t meet again— unless you leap it, leaving behind you the cherished worms of your dispassion, your pallid ironies, your jovial, murderous, wry-humored balanced judgment, leap over, un- balanced? ... then how our fanatic tears would flow and mingle for joy ...

Keywords: Genial, Cherries, Jubilee

outputs.L1:
Genial poets, pink-faced, earnest wits—you have given the world choice morsels, gobbets of language presented as one presents T-bone steak and Cherries Jubilee. Goodbye, goodbye. I do not care if I never taste your fine food again, neutral fellows, seers of every side. Tolerance—what crimes are committed in your name.

And you, good women, bakers of the nicest bread, donors of blood: your crumbs choke me. I would not want a drop of your blood in me; it is pumped by weak hearts, by perfect pulses that never falter, unresponsive to nightmare reality. It is the blood of my brothers, my sisters, that spurts out and stops forever because you choose to believe it is none of your business.

Goodbye, goodbye. Your poems shut their little mouths; your loaves grow moldy. A gulf has split the ground between us, and you will not wave—you are looking the other way. We shall not meet again—unless you leap across it, leaving behind the cherished worms of your dispassion, your pallid ironies, your jovial, murderous, wryly humorous, balanced judgment. Leap over, unbalanced—then how our fanatic tears would flow and mingle for joy.
outputs.L2:
Warmhearted poets and rosy, solemn intellectuals—you have offered the world exquisite fragments of expression, serving words as ceremoniously as prime steak and flaming dessert. Yet farewell: I have no wish ever to sample your delicacies again, you impartial observers and interpreters of every viewpoint. How much wrongdoing has been excused under the banner of tolerance.

And farewell to you, virtuous women who bake excellent bread and donate blood. Your smallest offerings stick in my throat. I want none of your blood inside me; it circulates through timid hearts and beats with flawless regularity, untouched by the horror of the real world. Meanwhile, the blood of my brothers and sisters bursts from their bodies and ceases to flow forever, because you have decided their suffering does not concern you.

Farewell. Your poems fall silent, your bread decays, and the earth has opened into a chasm between us. You do not even signal goodbye, because your eyes are turned elsewhere. We will never encounter one another again—unless you jump across that divide, abandoning the treasured parasites of your detachment, your bloodless sarcasm, and your cheerful, lethal, dryly amused impartiality. If you crossed over and surrendered your precious balance, then our passionate tears would meet and mingle in joy.
outputs.L3:
The speaker rejects artists and intellectuals whose eloquence, wit, and creativity remain detached from urgent moral realities. Verbal brilliance has little value when it fails to confront violence, suffering, and injustice. Indeed, the speaker regards supposedly admirable qualities such as tolerance, neutrality, and balanced judgment with suspicion. In moments of moral crisis, these attitudes are not signs of wisdom or fairness; instead, they become forms of complicity, allowing cruelty to continue without resistance.

This condemnation is sharpened by the contrast between the comfortable “goodness” of respectable people and the suffering of those they choose to ignore. Their civility and moral self-image are sustained at a terrible cost: while they remain calm, reasonable, and secure, others endure persecution and death. Their goodness is therefore exposed as shallow because it demands no sacrifice and does nothing to protect the vulnerable.

As a result, a profound moral gulf separates the speaker from those who look away and claim that the pain of others is not their concern. Their refusal to become involved represents more than a difference of opinion; it reveals a fundamental conflict over responsibility, empathy, and justice. Reconciliation can occur only if the indifferent abandon their detached neutrality. They must allow themselves to be emotionally affected, recognize the urgency of others’ suffering, and take a clear, committed stand against injustice.
outputs.L4:
The poem delivers a fierce condemnation of those who remain detached while other human beings endure violence, hunger, fear, and death. The speaker addresses artists, intellectuals, and respectable citizens who protect themselves behind neutrality, cultivated tolerance, or ironic distance. Their apparent moderation is not presented as wisdom or fairness; instead, it becomes a moral failure. By refusing to take sides when others are being destroyed, they effectively accept the conditions that allow such suffering to continue.

The speaker’s repeated farewells express both anger and sorrow. He separates himself from people whose art, learning, and social respectability have become excuses for passivity. Visceral images of wounded and suffering bodies sharply contrast with the abstract language of balance and objectivity. This contrast exposes the cruelty hidden beneath civilized manners: while some debate, observe, or make elegant judgments, others experience pain directly. The supposedly neutral spectators may not inflict the wounds themselves, but their indifference makes them complicit.

As a result, a profound gulf opens between the speaker and those he denounces. Their refusal to recognize the urgency of suffering makes genuine companionship seem impossible, and the separation feels almost permanent. Yet the poem does not end in complete despair. Its bitterness contains an appeal: reconciliation could still occur if detached observers abandoned their false impartiality and chose active solidarity. If they allowed compassion to overcome irony, accepted moral responsibility, and stood beside the oppressed, the speaker could welcome them again. The poem therefore imagines a future in which separation gives way to shared commitment and even joy—but only after neutrality has been replaced by courageous human fellowship.
outputs.L5:
### A Genial Cherries Jubilee

The evening ended on a brilliant note when our genial host appeared with a silver pan of Cherries Jubilee. Dark cherries shimmered in a rich, ruby sauce as he warmed them gently, then added a splash of brandy. With a practiced flourish, he struck a match, and blue flames danced across the fruit.

Everyone applauded as the warm cherries were spooned over vanilla ice cream. Sweet, tart, creamy, and dramatic, the dessert captured the spirit of the celebration perfectly—a little elegance, a little excitement, and plenty of joy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fierce prose poem condemning political neutrality and privileged detachment in the face of violence and injustice.
counterfactuals.output:
Do not call your silence peace.

Peace does not stand at the window while the street fills with blood, admiring the symmetry of both sides. Peace does not weigh the boot against the throat and declare the matter complicated. Your neutrality is not clean. It is a white glove laid over the mouth of the wounded. It is the locked door, the curtained room, the dinner kept warm while sirens comb the dark.

You say you refuse division, as if the blade and the flesh are equally guilty for the wound. You say you need more facts while graves are being dug with the names already spelled. You say politics is ugly because ugliness has never kicked in your door, never emptied your cupboards, never made your child memorize the route past the checkpoint.

Detachment is a throne built from other people’s emergencies.

Every tyrant treasures the citizen who will not choose. Every executioner praises the calm observer. Injustice does not ask for your devotion; it asks only for your patience, your doubt, your elegant hesitation. It fattens on the pause between seeing and speaking.

So step down from the balcony. Tear the neutrality from your face. There is no innocent distance from a burning house: you are carrying water or guarding the match. And history, with its terrible memory, will not ask whether you were comfortable, courteous, or above it all.

It will ask where you stood.

It will ask whom your silence served.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an impassioned farewell addressed to genial poets, well-meaning women, and “balanced” intellectuals who look away while others suffer.
counterfactuals.output:
Farewell, genial poets—  
you who polish moonlight into metaphors  
while the streets fill with smoke,  
who praise the human spirit  
but avert your eyes from human bodies  
bent beneath the boot.

Farewell, well-meaning women—  
tender in speech, charitable at table,  
who sigh over suffering at a safe distance  
and call silence kindness,  
who fear the raised voice more than the raised fist  
and counsel patience to those already bleeding.

Farewell, “balanced” intellectuals—  
accountants of agony,  
forever weighing the victim against the tormentor,  
finding fault on both sides of the wound.  
You stand at the edge of the fire  
and congratulate yourselves  
for not becoming flame.

Keep your measured phrases,  
your tasteful grief,  
your spotless consciences.  
Others have no shelter in moderation,  
no refuge in your careful doubts.  
They are hungry now.  
They are hunted now.  
They are dying while you debate the proper name for death.

I go to those whose voices crack from shouting,  
whose hands are rough from lifting the fallen,  
whose hope is not decorum  
but bread, breath, and freedom.

Farewell.  
When the hour asks what you did,  
may your eloquence answer for you—  
if it can.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a modernist free-verse monologue that uses food, blood, and a widening gulf as metaphors for the speaker’s rejection of passive liberals.
counterfactuals.output:
I will not dine at your table again.

The soup is always cooling  
while you debate the fire—  
whether flame is civil,  
whether hunger has consulted the proper forms.

You pass the bread clockwise.  
You call this progress.

Outside, the century  
keeps its red appointment.  
Blood writes quickly  
where your ink petitions pause;  
it enters the gutter,  
finds every low place,  
does not wait for consensus.

You blanch at the stain  
but not the wound.

Between us, the table lengthens—  
a white cloth drawn over a continent,  
plates diminishing into moons,  
your careful voices arriving late  
from the opposite shore.

You say: patience.  
I hear the knife being polished  
in another room.

You say: reason.  
I taste iron.

Now the gulf widens—  
not water, but appetite;  
not distance, but the knowledge  
that you would measure the abyss  
before building a bridge,  
appoint a committee  
to name the falling.

Keep your mild supper,  
your napkins folded like surrender.

I choose the raw hour,  
the bitter root,  
the salt that enters every cut.

If I cross back at all,  
it will not be to sit quietly.

It will be to overturn the table  
and let the empty dishes  
speak.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a bitter, lyrical denunciation of tolerance and dispassion, ending with the hope that neutral observers will finally abandon irony, cross the divide, and join the struggle.
counterfactuals.output:
Tolerance, they call it, as though every wound were merely weather, as though the boot and the throat beneath it deserved equal patience. Dispassion, they say, polishing their spectacles while the house burns—proud that no spark has troubled the cool republic of their blood.

But neutrality is not innocence. It is a balcony built above the flood, a clean handrail gripped while others drown. Irony is the last perfume of the comfortable: a clever scent sprayed over cowardice, so that retreat may pass for wisdom and silence for moral complexity.

Enough of this sterile grace. Enough of those who weigh a cry against the etiquette of crying, who condemn the broken window more swiftly than the long darkness behind it. There are hours when tolerance becomes surrender, when calm is merely fear with good posture, when refusing to choose is itself a choice—made quietly, reliably, for the stronger side.

Still, let us hope the watchers will tire of watching. Let them lay down their smirks, their elegant doubts, their safe and bloodless distance. Let them descend from the gallery, cross the divide, and discover at last that history is not a spectacle but a summons—and that the struggle has been waiting for their names.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
